claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by precise synchronization of reduction or thermal decomposition of all constituent precursors.
Simultaneous ligand loss and reduction cause simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous precursor conversion and nucleation yield homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Synchronized precursor conversion maximizes catalytically active surface sites.
Any mismatch in precursor-conversion kinetics leads to phase separation and elemental segregation.
Ligand engineering can make multiple noble-metal complexes decompose within narrowly defined and overlapping temperature ranges.
Engineering precursor formulations can synchronize their decomposition and reduction rates under a reductive thermal environment.
Real-time monitoring and processing adjustments can ensure the required temporal overlap of reduction events.
A moderate-temperature hydrogen or forming-gas environment can cause all ligands to break and all metal ions to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Simultaneous nucleation produces a uniform dispersion of metal atoms during the early stages of nanoparticle formation.
Synchronizing precursor conversion limits atomic or precursor mobility.
Limiting precursor mobility suppresses phase segregation and favors single-phase HEA formation.
Sequential, asynchronous reduction promotes elemental segregation.
Synchronized conditions will produce more uniform, single-phase nanoparticles than an asynchronous baseline.
Synchronized conditions will reduce particle growth and segregation, thereby increasing catalytic surface exposure relative to the baseline.
Unsynchronized precursor formulations produce heterogeneous nucleation, phase-separated structures, and reduced catalytic surface exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies when noble-metal precursor ligands and decomposition kinetics can be tightly controlled.
The mechanism may fail when reduction-potential differences cannot be overcome by precursor design or when high atomic mobility dominates.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis categorically states that any kinetic mismatch causes phase separation and segregation, while the uncertainty field says the effect of minor timing mismatches remains unknown.
